{: .fixed }
> - The "1% rule" isn't stated in any SR3 book checked, so it's been
>   removed.
> - "Astral Gateway collapse" isn't an SR3 hazard. **Focus addiction** is
>   real. *(MitS p.45)*
> - The Scenario C total was wrong: 8,000 × 3, then +100%, is **48,000¥**, not
>   32,000–40,000¥.
> - The **1,000¥ per point of Force** for hermetic conjuring materials was
>   correct. *(SR3 p.186; MitS p.169)*

pdf.quote: The summoning ritual also requires special ritual materials, available from a talismonger for approximately

entries.note: Errata callout. Focus addiction is a real MitS rule (printed p.45; the page's footer number is missing from its text layer so it cannot be recorded as evidence) and elemental conjuring materials cost about Force × 1,000¥ (SR3 p.186); neither is implemented. The Scenario C figure checks: 8,000 × 3 × 2 = 48,000.

entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / general description — states no rule

entries.text:
- **Drain**: casting above your Magic makes it **Physical**, and so does
  casting while astrally projecting. *(SR3 p.162)*

pdf.quote: If the Force of the spell is greater than the caster's Magic Attribute, the Drain causes physical damage
All spells cast while astrally projecting cause physical damage, regardless of Force

entries.text:
- **Magic loss**: on a Deadly wound, or medical treatment without the
  Awakened modifier, roll 2D6. At or under your Magic, you lose a point
  permanently. *(SR3 p.129)*

pdf.quote: The character's player rolls 2D6. If the result is less than or equal to the magician's current Magic Rating

entries.text:
- **Astral combat**: wounds taken on the astral appear on the body. Being
  disrupted forces a Magic Loss check. *(SR3 p.175)*
entries.reason: Astral damage appearing on the physical body and disruption forcing a Magic Loss check are on printed p.175, an image-only page (no text layer). Read via the SR-OCR dump: 'The physical body manifests any damage inflicted on the astral form' and 'A character who is disrupted in astral combat must immediately check for Magic Loss (p. 160)' — the guide agrees. The Magic Loss check for disruption is not implemented.

entries.text:
- **The law**: magic of **Force 3+** is regulated in the UCAS and CAS, and a
  felony committed with magic is treated as premeditated. *(MitS p.11)*
entries.reason: Legal background with no code counterpart. Checked against MitS printed p.11: Force 3+ magic is regulated in the UCAS and CAS, and a felony committed with magic is treated as premeditated; the guide agrees.

> - SR3 security codes are **Blue, Green, Orange and Red**, plus unofficial
>   "UV". There are no "Yellow" systems, and "Passive / Passive-Alert IC" is
>   not an IC type. *(SR3 p.205)*
> - **Blaster, sparky and tar pit are gray IC**: they damage the deck and its
>   programs. **Black IC** is the kind that hurts the decker, including the
>   psychotropic variety. *(SR3 p.227–230)*
> - The "Scenario C" total was right. The others are restated below with the
>   formula from [the hiring overview](../#the-house-rule-framework).

pdf.quote: Green (average security), Orange (significant security), and Red (high security)
the decker must spend a Complex Action and make a successful Willpower (Black IC Rating) Test to jack out

entries.note: Errata callout. Security codes Blue/Green/Orange/Red plus unofficial 'UV' (printed p.205) is implemented for the Orthodox host sheet; blaster, sparky and tar pit are gray IC and black IC hurts the decker (pp.227-230) is not (the Orthodox IC sheet has no Tar Pit type and no black-IC handling — see rules/combat.md #146, #147).

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> - There's no adept power called "Authoritative Voice". The SR3 powers are
>   **Commanding Voice** and **Kinesics**. *(SOTA64 p.64–66)*
> - A Rating 4–6 fake ID doesn't cost "1,000–10,000¥". By the Creating a
>   Credstick Table it's **16,000¥ at Rating 4 and 30,000¥ at Rating 6**.
>   *(SR3 p.239)*
> - *Corporate Download* is a real SR3 book, but it isn't in the library used
>   for checking. Nothing on this page depends on it.
entries.reason: Composite errata callout. Commanding Voice (SOTA64 p.64-65) and Kinesics (p.66) exist and 'Authoritative Voice' is absent from the core text; a Rating 4 fake ID costs 16,000¥ and Rating 6 costs 30,000¥ by the Creating a Credstick Table (p.239, agrees); Corporate Download is not in the library. Fake IDs are not modelled in the system.

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> **About the original eight hiring gists.** They credited their rates to a
> core-rulebook section called "Spells, Contacts, and Services". **No such
> section exists, and no SR3 book prices specialists by skill rating.** The
> books price **jobs**: see the Baseline Payment Table below. The day rates
> on the specialist pages are kept, marked as **house rules**, with the
> example arithmetic corrected. Several of the original examples didn't add
> up.

entries.reason: Game-master guidance about how Mr. Johnson pays (MJLBB printed pp.20-21); no code counterpart. entries.text: ## The house-rule framework
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / heading / table header / horizontal rule / index or method text — states no game rule

entries.text:
{: .house }
> The specialist pages use this structure. It came from the original gists.
> The numbers are **not from any SR3 book**, and are **much higher** than the
> Companion's baselines. For example, a "professional" bodyguard at
> 1,500¥ a night compares with the book's **200¥ a day**. They fit a
> high-paying campaign. Scale them to your table.
entries.reason: House-rule framework (the guide marks it as not from any SR3 book)

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> - The power is **Improved Reflexes** (levels 1–3, +1D6 to +3D6 Initiative),
>   not "Increased Reflexes". Its bonus **can't be combined** with wired
>   reflexes or other technological or magical boosts. *(SR3 p.169)*
> - Initiative dice aren't Initiative Passes. The number of passes comes from
>   the Initiative score, which drops by 10 each pass. *(SR3 p.104)*
> - There are no adept powers called "Invisibility" or "Silence". For stealth,
>   look at **Traceless Walk** *(MitS p.151)* and **Melanin Control**
>   *(SOTA64 p.67–68)*.
> - "Wall-walking" is **Wall Running**. "Bushido / Way powers" isn't an SR3
>   term, so it's been removed.
> - The Scenario C total was wrong: 18,000 × 4, then +50%, is **108,000¥**,
>   not 81,000¥.
entries.reason: Composite errata callout. Improved Reflexes (levels 1-3) not combining with technological or magical boosts (SR3 p.169) is implemented (SR3EActor.reflexBonus); initiative passes dropping 10 a pass (p.104) is implemented; Traceless Walk (MitS p.151), Melanin Control (SOTA64 p.67) and Wall Running (SOTA64 p.68) exist at the cited pages; 'Invisibility' and 'Silence' are spells, not adept powers, in the core rulebook. The Scenario C figure checks: 18,000 × 4 × 1.5 = 108,000.

# Hiring a Shaman
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / general description — states no rule

entries.text:
1. TOC
{:toc}
entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / general description — states no rule

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> - Shamans summon **nature spirits** of **Man, Land, Sky and Waters**, not
>   "domain spirits". They can only summon inside the spirit's domain, and a
>   nature spirit **can't leave its domain**. *(SR3 p.184, p.266–267)*
> - A spirit gives **one service per success** on the Conjuring Test, and
>   nature spirits **vanish at sunrise and sunset**. So "bring pre-summoned
>   spirits to the job" has a hard time limit. *(SR3 p.186)*
> - The Scenario C total was wrong: 8,000 × 3, then +50% and +100%, is
>   **60,000¥**, not 36,000–44,000¥.

pdf.quote: There are four classes of nature spirits
Nature spirits vanish at sunrise and sunset, no matter what

entries.note: Errata callout. Nature spirits come in four classes (Man, Land, Sky, Waters — printed p.266), can be summoned only in the spirit's domain (p.184) and vanish at sunrise and sunset (p.186), one service per Conjuring success (p.186). The system has some of the spirit types but does not enforce the domain or the sunrise/sunset limit (see magic/awakened-primer.md #21, #23). The Scenario C figure checks: 8,000 × 3 × (1 + .5 + 1) = 60,000.

  spirits. *(SR3 p.163–165)*

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> - **Wired reflexes give Initiative dice, not passes.** Levels 1/2/3 are
>   +2/+4/+6 Reaction and +1D6/+2D6/+3D6 Initiative. The number of passes
>   comes from the Initiative score. *(SR3 p.104, p.302)*
> - "Booster" means **boosted reflexes**, and "move booster" means
>   **move-by-wire**. *(SR3 p.302; M&M p.60)*
> - SR3 has **dermal plating** and **dermal sheath**; "subdermal plating" is
>   a later-edition name. *(SR3 p.302; M&M)*
> - The Scenario B and C totals were wrong. The correct figures are
>   **15,000¥** and **42,000¥**.

pdf.quote: the gamemaster subtracts 10 from each character's Initiative Score
Each level adds +2 to the user's Reaction and gives +1D6 Initiative die

code.snippet: for (let score = base; score > 0; score -= 10, pass++)

entries.note: Errata callout. Wired reflexes give +2/+4/+6 Reaction and +1D6/+2D6/+3D6 Initiative, not extra passes (printed p.104, p.301); the passes come from the score dropping by 10 each pass. The Scenario B and C totals check: 5,000 × 2 × 1.5 = 15,000 and 7,000 × 4 × 1.5 = 42,000.

# Primer for the Awakened
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
What a starting magician can do, how astral space works, and what an elven
mage in Seattle knows about the world.
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
1. TOC
{:toc}
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Primer for the Awakened Elf".
> - Drain codes like "4L, 3M, 5H" don't exist. SR3 writes Drain as `+1(M)`,
>   meaning Power = Force ÷ 2 + 1 at Moderate. There is no "H" level.
> - Force is capped by **the Force you learned the spell at**, not by your
>   Magic. Casting above your Magic is legal; the Drain just becomes Physical.
> - Nature spirits come in **four** families: Man, Land, Sky and Waters.
>   "Aura Masking" is not a spirit service.
> - SR3 ritual sorcery uses a **material link**. "Sympathetic link" is a term
>   from a later edition.
> - Astral attacks use an **Astral Combat Pool** and Sorcery, Unarmed Combat
>   or an armed skill with a weapon focus. The gist's "Astral Combat + Combat
>   Pool" was wrong. **Force / Magic is not astral armor.**
> - Projecting movement: normal speed is **Intelligence × 4 m per turn**, and
>   fast movement is up to **Magic in kilometers per turn**, not a flat
>   100 km per turn.
> - The Awakening is dated **24 December 2011**, when the dragon Ryumyo
>   appeared near Mount Fuji. It was not 21 December.

pdf.quote: Projecting characters and spirits have an Astral Combat Pool equal to the sum of their Mental Attributes, divided by two and rounded down
Fast movement is very fast! Your astral form can move up to a number of kilometers equal to your Magic Attribute in a single turn
There are four classes of nature spirits

entries.note: Composite errata callout. Checked against the book: Drain written +1(M) (p.191) and no 'H' level; Force capped by the Force learned (p.178) with Physical Drain above Magic (p.183); four nature-spirit classes Man/Land/Sky/Waters (p.266); material link in ritual sorcery (MitS); astral combat uses the Astral Combat Pool (p.174); projecting movement Intelligence x 4 m and Magic km per turn (p.173); Ryumyo seen on 24 December 2011 (p.25, p.269).

- **Casting** is a Complex Action: roll **Sorcery** plus up to as many
  **Spell Pool** dice as Sorcery dice. The TN is the target's **Willpower**

entries.note: Same two gaps as magic/spellcasting.md #7 and #43: the Spell Pool cap ('no more pool dice than Sorcery dice') and the Object Resistance Table are not implemented. Casting itself is a Complex Action and the Willpower/Body target numbers are.

entries.text:

entries.text: ### The Awakened world
entries.reason: section heading / table header row

entries.text:
- **The Awakening** happened in **2011**. On **24 December**, passengers on
  a bullet train saw the great dragon **Ryumyo** appear near Mount Fuji.
  *(SR3 p.25)*
entries.reason: World lore, no code counterpart. Checked against the book: the Ryumyo appeared near Mount Fuji on 24 December 2011 (printed p.25 and p.269); the guide agrees.

entries.text:
- **Traditions**: mages treat magic as a discipline of formulae and elements.
  *(SR3 p.158)* Shamans follow a **totem**, which grants bonus dice for some
  spells and spirits and penalties for others. *(SR3 p.163–165)*

pdf.quote: Hermetic magic is intellectual. Mages see the universe as a complex pattern of forces that can be controlled with the right formulae and rituals
A shaman gains bonus dice when using Sorcery or Conjuring according to the totem's ideals. The shaman may also lose dice when using magical skills outside the totem's realm

entries.text:
- **Essence and Magic**: every full point of Essence lost, or fraction of
  one, costs a point of **Magic**. Cyberware is the usual cause. *(SR3
  p.160)*

pdf.quote: one point for every full point of Essence, or fraction thereof

entries.text:
- **Magic and the law**: in the UCAS and CAS, any spell, spirit or focus of
  **Force 3 or higher is legally regulated**, and permits are available.

## Step 1: Preparation  *(SR3 p.178, p.181, p.191)*
{: #step-1-preparation }

pdf.quote: Choose the spell or spells to be cast, the Force of the spell, how many Spell Pool dice will be used

code.snippet: // Step 1: Choose Force (+ Damage Level, + area radius for AoE spells)

entries.text: Decide all of these before rolling.

pdf.quote: Choose the spell or spells to be cast, the Force of the spell, how many Spell Pool dice will be used

code.snippet: // Step 1: Choose Force (+ Damage Level, + area radius for AoE spells)

entries.text:
- **The spell and its Force.** You can cast at the Force you learned it at
  or lower, never higher. The minimum is Force 1. *(SR3 p.178)* Higher Force
  is harder to resist and produces more Drain.

pdf.quote: can never cast the spell at a higher Force than they have learned. The minimum Force for any spell is 1
The higher the Force of a spell, the greater its potential effect and the harder it is for the target to resist

entries.text:
- **Damage Level, for combat and elemental spells.** You choose **L, M, S or
  D** when you cast. That choice is both the spell's base damage **and** its
  base Drain Level. *(SR3 p.191, p.196)*

pdf.quote: The caster chooses the spell's Base Damage Level when it is cast, which also determines the base Drain Level

entries.text:
- **How many Sorcery dice** go into this spell, and how many **Spell Pool**
  dice. You can't add more pool dice than Sorcery dice. *(SR3 p.180)*

pdf.quote: No more Spell Pool dice can be used than the number of Sorcery dice allocated to the test

entries.text:
- **More than one spell?** You can split Sorcery and Spell Pool dice to cast
  several spells in one Complex Action, up to your Sorcery rating in spells,
  with at least 1 Sorcery die each. Each spell then gets **+2 to its Drain
  TN for every extra spell**. Two spells means +2 on each Drain Test; three
  means +4 on each. *(SR3 p.181)*

pdf.quote: The caster receives a +2 target number modifier for each extra spell to the Drain Resistance Test for all of the spells

entries.note: The system casts one spell per Complex Action. Splitting Sorcery and Spell Pool dice across several spells, the Sorcery-rating limit on how many, and the +2 Drain TN per extra spell do not exist.

entries.text:
- **Sustaining anything?** Choose whether to keep or drop spells you're
  already sustaining. Each one you keep costs **+2 to all your tests**,
  including this Sorcery Test and its Drain Test. *(SR3 p.178)*

pdf.quote: Characters sustaining spells have a +2 target modifier per sustained spell applied to all tests, including Drain Resistance Tests

entries.text:
- **Area spells**: the base radius is your **Magic in meters**, and it hits
  everyone valid inside, **including you and your friends**. Withhold
  Sorcery dice to change it: **every 2 dice withheld shrink it by 1 m**, or
  **every 1 die withheld widens it by 1 m**. *(SR3 p.181)*

pdf.quote: Area spells affect all valid targets within the radius of effect, friend and foe alike (including the caster)
every die withheld from the Sorcery Test increases the radius by 1 meter

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 171). The caster is now included (_actorsInRadius no longer filters a.id === caster.id), and the radius is computed from withheld Sorcery dice via spellAreaRadius (narrow: 1m per 2 dice withheld; widen: 1m per die withheld), read at cast time.

## Step 2: Targeting  *(SR3 p.181–182)*
{: #step-2-targeting }

pdf.quote: the caster must be able to see the target and must be present on the same plane

entries.text:
- You must **see** the target, and be **on the same plane** (physical or
  astral). Glasses, mirrors, fiber optics and cybereyes are fine. **Any
  digital image**, such as a camera feed, simsense or a vision-altering spell
  like Clairvoyance, is not. *(SR3 p.181)*

pdf.quote: An opaque barrier prevents the caster from seeing the target
prevents the caster from casting spells on that target

entries.note: Line of sight, plane, glass and opaque barriers are the GM's call: targets are picked from a list or found by radius, with no sight or barrier check.

entries.text:
- **Glass** doesn't stop most spells, because the effect happens at the
  target and nothing travels. An **opaque** barrier blocks the spell.
  *(SR3 p.182)*

pdf.quote: An opaque barrier prevents the caster from seeing the target
prevents the caster from casting spells on that target

entries.note: Line of sight, plane, glass and opaque barriers are the GM's call: targets are picked from a list or found by radius, with no sight or barrier check.

entries.text:
- **Touch-range spells** skip cover and visibility modifiers, but you must
  touch the target first with an Unarmed Combat attack at −1 TN, as part of
  the same action. One net success is enough. *(SR3 p.178, p.183)*

pdf.quote: One net success is sufficient for the caster to touch the target
Spells with a range of touch are not subject to cover or visibility modifiers

entries.text:
- **From the astral**, you can only cast **mana** spells, and only at astral
  targets. **Astrally perceiving** casters can target both planes, but can be
  attacked from both. *(SR3 p.182)*

pdf.quote: Astral targets (including dual beings) can only be affected by mana spells

entries.text: ### Modifiers to the Sorcery TN  *(SR3 p.182–183)*

pdf.quote: Likewise, distractions such as injury modifiers

entries.text: - **Cover and visibility**, as for Perception.

pdf.quote: the target number of the spell increases

pdf.quote: and sustaining other spells increase the target number

entries.text: ### Results
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text: - **No successes:** the spell fails.

pdf.quote: If there are no successes, the spell fails and there is no effect

code.snippet: // Drain button always — caster pays drain regardless of hit/miss

entries.text: - **All 1s:** it fails **and** your Drain TN goes up by **+2**. *(SR3 p.182)*

pdf.quote: If the results are all ones (see Rule Of One, p. 38), the spell fails and the target number for the Drain Resistance Test is increased by +2

entries.text:

entries.text:
## Step 4: Spell Resistance  *(SR3 p.183)*
{: #step-4-spell-resistance }

pdf.quote: Living targets may always make a Spell Resistance Test

entries.text:
Two different things can reduce the caster's successes here. Both can happen
against the same spell.
entries.reason: introductory sentence; the two mechanisms it announces (target resists, spell defense) are checked in the units below

entries.text: ### The target resists
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
- Any **living** target that isn't **willing** makes a **Spell Resistance
  Test**: its **targeted attribute** (usually Body, Intelligence or
  Willpower) against **TN = the spell's Force**.

pdf.quote: Living targets may always make a Spell Resistance Test against spells, unless the target of the spell is willing

entries.note: A resistance test is offered to every live target; the exception for a willing target ('unless the target of the spell is willing') is not modelled.

entries.text:
- **No modifiers apply** unless the spell says so. That includes the
  target's wounds. *(SR3 p.183)*

pdf.quote: No target modifiers apply to this test except where specifically noted

entries.text: - **Non-living, non-magical** targets don't resist.

pdf.quote: Non-living, non-magical targets may not make a Resistance Test

entries.text:
> **How The 2nd Chumming reads it:** a target who is **sustaining spells**
> still takes **+2 per spell** on this test. The book says both "no target
> modifiers apply to this test" *(SR3 p.183)* and that sustaining costs +2 on
> "all tests, including Drain Resistance Tests (but not normal Damage
> Resistance Tests)" *(SR3 p.178)*. The maintainer ruled that p.178's "all
> tests" wins (2026-09-14). Wounds still don't apply.
{: .house }

pdf.quote: No target modifiers apply to this test except where specifically noted
Characters sustaining spells have a +2 target modifier per sustained spell applied to all tests, including Drain Resistance Tests (but not normal Damage Resistance Tests)

entries.note: House-rule callout documenting the maintainer's 2026-09-14 ruling that resolves a real conflict between p.178 ('all tests') and p.183 ('no target modifiers except where noted'): handleSpellResistRoll sets skipWoundMod but not skipSustainMod, so rollPool applies the sustaining +2 to the Spell Resistance Test while wounds are excluded, matching the stated ruling.

entries.text: ### A magician blocks it: Spell Defense  *(SR3 p.183)*

pdf.quote: Sorcery can be used to defend against the effects of spells as well as cast them

entries.text:
- At some earlier point, a magician **set aside Sorcery and Spell Pool dice
  for defense**. That's a Free Action.

pdf.quote: Allocating Spell Defense dice is a Free Action

entries.text:
- They can protect up to **their Sorcery rating** in subjects, all within
  **Magic × 100 m** and on the same plane. Protecting yourself counts as one.

pdf.quote: within a distance equal to the caster's Magic Attribute x 100 meters, can be protected
A character can protect a maximum number of subjects equal to their Sorcery Skill Rating

entries.note: A mage's Spell Defense pool is one total for the Combat Turn. Who is protected, the Sorcery-rating limit on subjects, the Magic × 100 m range and the same-plane condition are not recorded; every defender with a pool is offered a Counterspelling roll against any spell.

entries.text:
- When a protected subject is targeted, the defender **senses it** and may
  roll any of those dice against **TN = the spell's Force**. It takes no
  action.

pdf.quote: Any Spell Defense dice the magician wishes to use are rolled against a target number equal to the Force of the spell

code.snippet: state._pendingDefenseCard = { currentSuccesses: bestHits, sc, force: sc.force };

entries.text:
- **Every success subtracts one success from the caster's Sorcery Test.** If
  that takes the caster to **0 or less**, the spell fails.

pdf.quote: Any successes subtract directly from the successes the spell's caster achieves on the Sorcery Test

entries.text: - Dice used are **gone until the next Combat Turn**.

pdf.quote: Once used, Spell Defense dice are lost until the magician's next Combat Turn

code.snippet: turn; Sorcery dice return at round end.

entries.text:
## Step 5: Spell Effect  *(SR3 p.183, p.191)*
{: #step-5-spell-effect }

pdf.quote: If the target generated the same number or more successes, the spell does not affect the target

entries.text:
Compare the caster's remaining successes with the target's resistance
successes.

pdf.quote: the caster's successes are compared to the successes generated by the target

entries.text: - **Target ties or wins:** **no effect.** A tie goes to the target.

pdf.quote: If the target generated the same number or more successes, the spell does not affect the target

entries.text:
- **Caster wins:** the **net successes** (caster − target) measure the
  effect. The spell's description says what they buy.

pdf.quote: The spell's effect is measured as the difference between the caster's successes and the target's

entries.text:
- **No resistance roll** (an object, or a willing subject): all the caster's
  successes count, and **1 success always gives some effect**.

pdf.quote: When casting spells against non-resisting targets (which are generally non-living targets) one success always insures some degree of effect

entries.text:
- **Damaging spells:** the chosen Damage Level **stages up one level per 2
  net successes**, up to Deadly.

pdf.quote: For any spells that damage the target, stage up the Damage Level for every 2 net successes

entries.text: ### Combat spells: armor doesn't help  *(SR3 p.191)*

pdf.quote: Combat spells ignore the effects of armor and nonmagical, external protections

code.snippet: //   Net successes (caster − resister) stage the base damage. No soak.

entries.text:
Combat spells (Manabolt, Powerbolt, Stunbolt and their ball versions)
damage the target **directly and bypass armor**. The Spell Resistance Test
is the target's only defense, so **there's no Damage Resistance Test**.
Mana spells are resisted with **Willpower** and affect only living and
magical targets. Physical spells are resisted with **Body** and can hit
objects too.

pdf.quote: Combat spells ignore the effects of armor and nonmagical, external protections
Only physical spells affect non-living objects

code.snippet: //   Net successes (caster − resister) stage the base damage. No soak.

entries.text: ### Elemental spells work like guns  *(SR3 p.183, p.196)*

pdf.quote: Elemental spells are treated like normal ranged attacks (see p. 109) using Sorcery as the Ranged Combat Skill

entries.text:
Fireball, Flamethrower, Lightning Bolt, Acid Stream and similar spells make
**real fire, lightning or acid**. They follow the ranged combat rules,
so steps 3 to 5 change:

pdf.quote: Elemental spells are treated like normal ranged attacks (see p. 109) using Sorcery as the Ranged Combat Skill

entries.text:
1. **Sorcery is the ranged combat skill.** The base TN is **4 at any range**
   if you can see the target, plus cover, visibility, injury and sustaining
   modifiers. Spell Pool dice can be added. *(SR3 p.183)*

pdf.quote: They have a base Target Number of 4, regardless of range, as long as the caster can see the target

code.snippet: return { tn: Math.max(2, numeric), resistAttr: 'willpower', resistName: 'Willpower', attrLabel: `Fixed ${numeric}` };

entries.text: 2. The target can **dodge** with Combat Pool. *(SR3 p.183)*

pdf.quote: These spells can be dodged

entries.text:
3. Instead of a Spell Resistance Test, the target makes a **Damage Resistance
   Test** with Body plus Combat Pool dice, and **Impact armor at half its
   rating** (rounded down) protects. *(SR3 p.183, p.196)*

pdf.quote: the Resistance Test is actually a Damage Resistance Test
Impact Armor protects against damage from elelmental manipulations, but at only half its normal rating (round down)

entries.text:
4. The chosen Damage Level stages up 2 successes per level for the caster
   and down for the target, as in ordinary ranged combat. *(SR3 p.183)*

pdf.quote: The Damage Level is staged up by every 2 successes the caster made on the Ranged Combat Test

entries.note: Follows the ranged flow, so it inherits the staging difference recorded at combat.md #50.

entries.text:
5. **Secondary effects** can still set fires, cook off ammunition or melt
   material, even if the primary damage is staged to nothing. *(SR3 p.196)*

pdf.quote: If, after applying the primary damage of the spell, anyone is left standing and in some way vulnerable to the secondary effects, roll 2D6

entries.text:
Glass and walls **do** block elemental spells, which have to break through
like bullets. Targets hidden behind cover inside a Fireball's radius **still
get hit**. Spell Defense and astral barriers still work against them.
*(SR3 p.182)*

pdf.quote: it is impeded by physical obstructions like glass and other barriers
Targets hidden behind a wall within the radius of a Fireball spell will still get cooked

entries.note: Elemental spells are not blocked by glass or walls in the code: nothing checks obstructions. (Everyone the area picks up is a target, which happens to match the 'hidden targets still get hit' half.)

entries.text: ## Worked example: Manabolt
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
Kestrel has **Magic 6**, **Sorcery 5**, and a Spell Pool of **4**
(Intelligence 5, Willpower 5, Magic 6 → 16 ÷ 3 = 5, and she spent 1 earlier
this turn). She casts **Manabolt at Force 5**, choosing **Serious**, at a
guard with Willpower **4**. She isn't sustaining anything.

pdf.quote: A character's Spell Pool is equal to Intelligence plus Willpower plus Magic Rating, divided by 3, rounded down

entries.text:
1. **Preparation.** Force 5, Serious, 5 Sorcery dice plus **3** Spell Pool
   dice. That leaves 1 pool die for Drain.

pdf.quote: Choose the spell or spells to be cast, the Force of the spell, how many Spell Pool dice will be used

entries.text: 2. **Targeting.** She can see him and they're both on the physical plane.

pdf.quote: the caster must be able to see the target and must be present on the same plane

entries.text:
3. **Sorcery Test.** 8 dice against **TN 4** (his Willpower). She gets **4
   successes**.

pdf.quote: the target number is usually the target's Willpower for a mana spell, or Body for a physical spell

entries.text:
4. **Resistance.** The guard rolls Willpower 4 against **TN 5** (the Force)
   and gets **1**. Nobody is running Spell Defense for him.

pdf.quote: The target number is the Force of the spell

entries.text:
5. **Effect.** 4 − 1 = **3 net successes**. Two of them stage Serious up to
   **Deadly**; the third is left over. Combat spells ignore armor, so the
   guard takes a **Deadly Physical** wound.

pdf.quote: For any spells that damage the target, stage up the Damage Level for every 2 net successes
Manabolt and Manaball channel destructive magical power into the target, doing physical damage

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 169) alongside #85: Manabolt now deals Physical, so the worked example's 'Deadly Physical wound' agrees with the code.

entries.text:
6. **Drain.** Manabolt's Drain is `(Damage Level)`. Power is 5 ÷ 2 = **2**,
   and the level is **Serious**, the level she *chose*, not the staged one.
   She rolls Willpower 5 plus her last Spell Pool die, 6 dice against TN
   **2**, and gets **3 successes**. Two of them take Serious down to
   **Moderate**. Force 5 isn't higher than her Magic 6, so it's **Moderate
   Stun**.

pdf.quote: The target number is the Force of the spell, divided by 2 (rounded down) plus any Drain Modifier to the spell's Drain Code

code.snippet: return { tn: Math.max(2, halfF + powerMod + abovePower), level };

entries.text:
**If she had cast at Force 7** (assuming she'd learned it that high):
Drain Power would be 3, and the Drain would be **Physical**, because 7 is
higher than her Magic.

pdf.quote: If the Force of the spell is greater than the caster's Magic Attribute, the Drain causes physical damage

entries.text:
**If a mage were protecting the guard** with Spell Defense and rolled 2
successes against TN 5, Kestrel's 4 would drop to **2**. The guard's 1
resistance success would leave **1 net success**: not enough to stage up,
so he'd take **Serious**.

pdf.quote: Any successes subtract directly from the successes the spell's caster achieves on the Sorcery Test

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Complete Actions & Combat System Guide".
> - You get **one Free Action in every Combat Phase**, including other
>   characters' phases, not one per Initiative Pass.
> - "Take Cover" is not an SR3 action. "Suppressive fire" is not a defined
>   action or modifier in the core rules; the phrase appears only in a rigger
>   example (SR3 p.156).
> - Nearly every value in the modifiers table was wrong: partial cover is
>   **+4**, target running is **+2**, and the visibility values come from a
>   two-axis table.
> - Damage staging is **net**: attacker successes are compared with the
>   defender's Dodge + Damage Resistance successes. The dodge doesn't reduce
>   the attacker's successes directly.
> - SR3 has a **Spell Pool**, not a Magic Pool. Drain TN is Force ÷ 2 plus a
>   modifier; there is no minimum-2 rule of its own.
> - Matrix: there is no "Access Node" action (the nearest is the **Locate
>   Access Node** operation, SR3 p.210) and no "Response Index". Hacking Pool
>   **cannot** be used to resist black IC.
> - Vehicles: "VCTR" is not an SR3 term. A crash test comes from **Serious**
>   damage in one attack, not Moderate, and the TN is Handling.

pdf.quote: A character may take a Free Action during their own Combat Phase and during the Combat Phase of any other character, as long as it is declared. Only one Free Action may be made by each character during any given Combat Phase

A character's Spell Pool is equal to Intelligence plus Willpower plus Magic Rating
Vehicle takes Serious damage in a single attack (including weapon and spell attacks)
The Crash Test consists of a Driving Test against a base target number equal to the vehicle's Handling Rating

entries.note: The book compares NET successes: p.113 'compare the successes rolled by the attacker and the target' and its worked example stages once for Liam's 2 net successes. The code does not net them. It stages UP by the attacker's raw successes (SR3EItem.stageDamage(state.damageBase, successes), SR3EActor.js:3233) and then stages DOWN separately by the defender's soak + carried dodge successes (floor(total/2), SR3EActor.js:4098). floor(A/2) − floor(D/2) is not floor((A−D)/2): attacker 2 vs defender 1 should be base damage (net 1) but the code stages up one level; attacker 4 vs 1 should stage up once (net 3) but the code stages up twice. p.114 also has a paragraph describing each side staging on its own successes ('usually compared'), so the code follows one reading of the book; the worked example follows the other. The maintainer's call which governs.

entries.text:
- Attacker ahead: stage the Damage Level **up** one step (L → M → S → D)
     per **2** successes over the defender's total.

pdf.quote: The base damage increases by one Damage Level for every two successes the attacker rolls over the target's total

entries.note: Same finding as #50: 'one step per 2 successes over the defender's total' is a net comparison; the code stages up by 2-per-level of the attacker's RAW successes before the defender's total is known.

entries.text:
- Defender ahead: stage it **down** one step per 2 successes over the
     attacker's. Below Light, no damage.

pdf.quote: the target can stage down the weapon's base Damage Level by one for every two successes the target rolls over the attacker's total

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 165). netStagedDamage takes the NET of attacker and defender successes and stages down by one level per 2 net successes in the defender's favour, replacing the old floor(total/2) reading.

entries.text: - Tie: base damage.

pdf.quote: If the attacker's successes equal the target's, the weapon does its base Damage Level

entries.note: A tie is base damage in the book. In the code a tie is base damage only while staging up does not hit the Deadly cap: attacker and defender both at 6 successes against a 9M attack stage up to 9D (surplus discarded) and then down three levels to Light instead of staying Moderate. Same root as #50.

entries.text: Casting a spell is a **Complex Action**. *(SR3 p.107)*

pdf.quote: A magician may cast a spell by taking a Complex Action

entries.text:
1. **Force**: you can cast a spell at any Force up to the one you learned it
   at, never higher. *(SR3 p.178)*

pdf.quote: can never cast the spell at a higher Force than they have learned

entries.text:
2. **Sorcery Test**: Sorcery dice plus up to an equal number of **Spell
   Pool** dice. The TN is the target's **Willpower** for mana spells or
   **Body** for physical spells. Objects use the Object Resistance Table:
   natural 3, low-tech 5, high-tech 8, highly processed 10+. *(SR3 p.182)*
   If every die shows 1, the spell fails and Drain TN rises by 2.
   *(SR3 p.182)*

pdf.quote: No more Spell Pool dice can be added to the test than the Sorcery dice allocated
Consult the Object Resistance Table for examples of objects and materials

entries.note: Implemented from this unit: the Sorcery Test against the target's Willpower (mana) or Body (physical), and the all-ones glitch adding +2 to the Drain TN (SR3EActor.js:9730). Not implemented: (1) the Object Resistance Table — there is no way to target an object and no object target numbers (natural 3, low-tech 5, high-tech 8, processed 10+); (2) the cap 'no more Spell Pool dice than Sorcery dice allocated' — the prompt offers everything available (SR3EItem.js:4548-4568, `_promptMagicPool(actor, availMagic)`).

entries.text:
Throwing or launching a grenade, where it lands, when it goes off, and what
the blast does. All rules are from the core rulebook, *(SR3 p.118–119)*.

pdf.quote: Resolving a grenade attack is a two-step process

entries.text:
1. TOC
{:toc}
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule (the description's SR3 pp.118-119 cite is for the whole page and is checked in the sections below)

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Grenade Throwing Rules Reference".
> - The range table was invented. Grenades have **their own** range table,
>   with base TNs **4 / 5 / 8 / 9**, not 4 / 5 / 6 / 9, and bands of STR × 3 /
>   5 / 10 / 20 for a standard grenade.
> - Scatter is **1D6 m** (standard), **2D6 m** (aerodynamic) or **3D6 m**
>   (launcher). Each success removes **2 m** (standard) or **4 m**
>   (aerodynamic and launcher), not 2D6 m less 1 m per success.
> - Grenades go off in **your next Combat Phase**, not at the end of the
>   Combat Turn. There are no fuse types in the core rules.
> - Offensive grenades are **10S, −1 Power per meter**. Defensive grenades
>   are **10S, −1 per half meter**. Concussion grenades are **12M Stun, −1
>   per meter**. There is no "12D HE".
> - All blast damage is resisted with **Impact** armor.
> - The chunky salsa effect adds the **combined Power** of each pass of the

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Healing Rules Reference".
> - **Stun**: TN is **2 plus your injury modifiers**, not 2 plus the number of
>   boxes filled. Recovering **one box** takes **60 minutes ÷ successes**. You
>   roll the **higher** of Body or Willpower; that's the rule, not a GM option.
> - **First aid**: TN is **4 / 6 / 8 / 10** by wound level. One success lowers
>   the wound **one Damage Level**, never more. It doesn't heal a box per
>   success, and there is no "capped by medkit rating".
> - **Heal / Treat**: TN is **10 − the patient's Essence**, not the number of
>   boxes filled. Each success heals **one box, up to the spell's Force**.
>   Heal has no +2 penalty after an hour.
> - **Natural healing** uses the Healing Table (TN 4 / 6 / 8 / 10), and the
>   base time is divided by your successes. The "nurse / hospital / DocWagon"
>   modifiers in the original were invented. The real ones are on the
>   Doctoring Table below.
> - The fourth level is **Deadly**, not "Lethal".

## Stun damage  *(SR3 p.126)*
{: #stun-damage }

pdf.quote: Healing Stun Damage Technically, overcoming Stun damage is more a process of recovery than healing

entries.text:
Stun runs on its own track and recovers much faster. **No medicine or known
spell helps**; you just rest.

pdf.quote: No medical treatment really helps to recover Stun damage, nor does any magical spell currently known to man

entries.text:
1. The **patient** rolls **Body or Willpower, whichever is higher**, against
   **TN 2**, plus current Stun and Physical injury modifiers.

pdf.quote: against a base Target Number 2. This target number is modified by any appropriate Stun or Physical injury modifiers

entries.text:
2. Recovering **one box** takes **60 minutes ÷ successes**. Erase the box,
   then roll again for the next one.

pdf.quote: The actual time it takes to recover 1 box of Stun damage is equal to the base time, divided by the number of successes rolled

entries.text:
3. The patient must be **resting completely**. If they're interrupted, they
   start over, and the new roll can't beat the first one.

pdf.quote: The result can never be better than the result of the first roll, however

entries.text:
# Cyberware Grades & Used Chrome
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
Basic, alpha, beta and deltaware; buying used; removing chrome; and selling
what you've pulled out. Grade rules are from *Man & Machine: Cyberware*.
entries.reason: page description

entries.text:
1. TOC
{:toc}
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Cyberware Grades & Secondhand Gear Guide".
> - **Betaware is ×.6 Essence**, not ×.7.
> - **Used cyberware costs the Essence of its grade**, not ×1.25. It costs
>   **half price**, not ×.75.
> - The availability modifiers were invented. Alphaware is **as available as
>   basic**. Betaware is **+5 to the TN and ×1.5 the time**. Deltaware is at
>   least **+9 and ×3**. Used is standard.
> - **Betaware isn't available to starting characters** either, not only
>   deltaware.
> - Used deltaware **can't be bought**, but if you get hold of some, it can
>   be **installed as betaware**. It isn't "destroyed on extraction".
> - Used implants come with **1D3 permanent Stress Points**, not "1 to 2".
> - **Removing** chrome never gives Essence back. A *later* implant can use
>   the "Essence hole", but only through a surgical option at +2 Threshold.
> - The 1–3 hour harvest window, the TN 4–8 extraction roll and the
>   "Electronics (Cyberware) scrub" aren't in *Man & Machine*.

pdf.quote: Beta Delta Used -40% (x .6) 4 -50% (x .5) 8 By grade .5 +5/x 1.5 +9/x 3 Standard
used cyberware begins with 1D6

entries.note: Composite errata callout; the code differs in two of its claims. (1) 'Used deltaware can be installed as betaware' — `gradedEssenceCost` strips the word 'used' and reads a Used Delta as delta (×.5), not beta (×.6). (2) 'Used implants come with 1D3 permanent Stress Points' (M&M p.45) — the Stress code starts used cyberware with 1D6 ÷ 2 rounded down (stress.mjs `pointsFromDie`), following M&M p.124's own wording ('1D6 ÷ 2'), so the book itself is inconsistent between p.45 and p.124. Also: 'betaware isn't available to starting characters' is not enforced. The other claims (beta ×.6, used at half price, +5/×1.5 and +9/×3 availability, removal gives no Essence back) are implemented.

entries.text: ## The four grades  *(M&M p.10–11)*

pdf.quote: Cyberware is available in four grades

entries.text: - **Basic** is mass-market and fits anyone. Any street doc can install it.

pdf.quote: Any surgeon or street doctor can implant basic cyberware

entries.text:
- **Alphaware** has better materials and testing. It's as easy to get as
  basic and costs twice as much.

pdf.quote: It is as readily available as basic cyberware, but it costs twice as much and also reduces Essence loss

- **Betaware** is custom-fitted to your body, after tests and DNA screening,
  and uses myomers in place of gyros and microengines. It must be
  special-ordered.

pdf.quote: Betaware must be special-ordered

entries.text:
- **Deltaware** is built during the surgery itself, in corporate clinics
  that are almost never mentioned. It isn't available on the street.

pdf.quote: Deltaware implants, parts and tools cost eight times as much as basic cyberware

entries.note: 'Isn't available on the street' is not enforced; the sheet offers Delta like any other grade.

entries.text: ## Used cyberware  *(M&M p.11, p.45)*

pdf.quote: Basic, alpha and beta cyberware is available used

entries.text:
- **Basic, alpha and beta** chrome can be bought used. It's cheap, it's of
  suspect quality, and it still works.

pdf.quote: Basic, alpha and beta cyberware is available used

entries.text:
- **Used deltaware can't be bought.** If you acquire some anyway, it's
  installed **as if it were betaware**.

pdf.quote: Used deltaware cannot be purchased, but if you can otherwise acquire it, you can have it installed as if it were betaware

entries.note: The book: 'Used deltaware cannot be purchased, but if you can otherwise acquire it, you can have it installed as if it were betaware.' The code strips 'used' from a grade and reads a Used Delta as delta (Essence ×.5), not as beta (×.6).

entries.text:
- Used chrome is **as easy to find as basic**, but the sellers are
  organleggers, ghouls and dubious clinics.

pdf.quote: Used cyberware is as easy to find as basic cyberware

entries.text:
- Its **Essence cost is the same as new of that grade**. Its **price is
  half**.

pdf.quote: Essence reductions and cost multipliers for alpha, beta, and delta-grade and used cyberware appear on the Cyberware Grades Table

entries.text:
- **Each used item comes with 1D3 permanent Stress Points.** They can never
  be removed, and they add to any Stress it picks up in use. *(M&M p.45; see
  Damage and Healing, M&M p.124)*

pdf.quote: Each used cyberware item comes with 1D3 permanent Stress Points
used cyberware begins with 1D6

entries.note: M&M p.45 says each used implant comes with 1D3 permanent Stress Points; M&M p.124 says used cyberware begins with 1D6 ÷ 2 permanent Stress Points. The code follows p.124 and rounds down (1D6 ÷ 2 → 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3), so a roll of 1 gives none and the spread differs from a flat 1D3. The book contradicts itself; the guide states the p.45 form.

entries.text: ## Selling harvested chrome
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
*Man & Machine* has no separate resale rule for used implants, so sell them
the same way as any other loot. Use the [fencing rules](../gear-and-fencing/#fencing-the-loot)
*(SR3 p.237–238)*: a **30%** base, **5% per net success** on the
Negotiation, never below **10%** or above **50%**. Stolen chrome isn't
standard gear, so expect the Finding a Fence TN to rise.

pdf.quote: The base price for most loot is 30 percent of its actual value
If the team won, the payment price will not rise above 50 percent of the actual value

entries.note: Resale of harvested chrome goes through the fencing rules, which are not built (see gear-and-fencing.md #43-70). The example arithmetic checks: 2,500 + 11,500 = 14,000; 30% = 4,200; 10% = 1,400; 50% = 7,000.

entries.text:

spur** (11,500¥) *(SR3 p.302)* list at **14,000¥** together. The fence's
base offer is **4,200¥**. Depending on the Negotiation, the deal can't go
below 1,400¥ or above 7,000¥.

# Buying Gear & Fencing
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
Availability, Street Index and Legality Codes; buying through contacts; and
selling stolen goods to a fence. All rules are from the core rulebook,
*(SR3 p.237–238, p.270–274)*.

pdf.quote: Availability is a measure of how easy it is to obtain the item on the street

entries.text:
1. TOC
{:toc}
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Gear Availability, Acquisition, & Fencing Guide".
> - SR3 Legality Codes look like **`6P-E`**, not "R" or "F". The number is
>   the restriction level, **P** means a permit is available, and the letter
>   is the category.
> - Successes on the acquisition test **divide** the base time. They don't
>   cut it by 25–50% each.
> - Paying to hurry a search costs **+2 days and +0.1 Street Index for each
>   −1 to the Availability TN**. It's not "+25–50% per die".
> - The price is **negotiated**: Negotiation against Intelligence, **5% per
>   net success**.
> - Fencing: the **30% base and 5% per net success** were right, but the
>   limits are a **10% floor and a 50% ceiling**, not 60%. The "chop shop 10–15%"
>   rate and the hot, encrypted and scarce percentage modifiers were invented.
>   The book handles risk through the **Finding a Fence** TN instead.
> - The **Ares Predator III** isn't in the core rulebook. The examples below
>   use the core **Ares Predator** (450¥, Availability 3/24 hrs, Street
>   Index .5).

pdf.quote: Whichever side wins the Negotiation Test alters the price paid in his or her favor by 5 percent per extra success
If the fence won, the payment price will not drop below 10 percent of the actual value

entries.note: Composite errata callout. What is implemented (Availability as TN / base time, successes dividing the time, −1 TN for 2 days and +0.1 Street Index, negotiation at 5% per net success) is checked at #9, #16-20. Not implemented: Legality Codes (the 6P-E notation is not stored on any pack item) and fencing, whose 30% base, 5% per net success, 10% floor and 50% ceiling are at #43-70. The 'Ares Predator III is not in the core rulebook' claim is true (no such entry in the text).

entries.text: ## Reading a gear entry  *(SR3 p.270–272)*

pdf.quote: Each piece of gear has an individual description and a table listing

entries.text: | Statistic | Meaning |
entries.reason: table header row

entries.text: | **Concealability** | TN for Perception Tests to spot it. Searches use half. |

pdf.quote: Searches have a target number of half the regular Concealability Rating (rounding down)

entries.text: | **Availability** | Two numbers: **TN / base time**, for example `3/24 hrs`. |

pdf.quote: The number to the left is a target number that represents the difficulty of obtaining the item; the one to the right represents the base time necessary to acquire it

entries.text: | **Cost** | The legal retail price in nuyen. |

pdf.quote: Cost is the base cost of the weapon in nuyen

entries.text: | **Street Index** | The black-market multiplier on Cost. |

pdf.quote: Street Index is the market value multiplier to the item's base cost

entries.text: | **Legality** | Restriction level, permit availability, and category. |

pdf.quote: Legality represents whether or not it is illegal to own the item, carry or transport it, what restriction category it falls into, and whether or not permits for the item are available

entries.note: A legality text field exists on a few item types (drugs, one other), but Legality Codes are not stored on weapons and gear and nothing interprets them.

entries.text:
At character creation, no gear may have a Device Rating above **6** or an
Availability above **8**. *(SR3 p.270)* Gear modified for a dwarf costs
**+10%**, and for a troll **+25%**. *(SR3 p.272)*

pdf.quote: no character may start the game with a piece of gear whose Availability is greater than 8

entries.note: The dwarf +10% / troll +25% surcharge is implemented (purchasing.mjs RACIAL_SURCHARGE). The character-creation limits (Device Rating at most 6, Availability at most 8) are not enforced.

entries.text: ## Buying on the street  *(SR3 p.272–273)*

pdf.quote: characters must use an appropriate contact

entries.text:
1. **Find a source.** Contact a fixer or other suitable contact and make an
   **Etiquette Test** against the **Availability TN**. Contacts differ: a
   talismonger is great for magical goods and poor for guns.

pdf.quote: the player gets in touch with a contact (usually a fixer) and makes an Etiquette Test
Talismongers, for example, are an ideal contact for magical items, but not very good at acquiring weapons

code.snippet: talismonger:  { good: ['focus', 'spell', 'magical'], bad: ['firearm', 'melee', 'projectile', 'ammunition'], note: 'ideal for magical items, poor for weapons (p.272)' },

entries.text:
2. **Wait.** **Base time ÷ successes** is how long it takes the source to
   find the item.

pdf.quote: The base time divided by the number of successes provides the actual time it takes the source to locate the item

entries.text:
3. **No successes?** The contact can't or won't find it. At the GM's
   discretion you can put the word out: **for each −1 to the Availability
   TN, add 2 days to the wait and +0.1 to the Street Index**. *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: the character may add 2 days to the acquisition time period and .1 to the Street Index (increasing the cost) in order to reduce the Availability target number by 1

code.snippet: export const REDUCTION = { daysPerPoint: 2, streetIndexPerPoint: 0.1, page: 'SR3 p.272' };

entries.text:
4. **Negotiate.** Halfway through the wait you meet the source. The asking
   price is **Cost × Street Index**, plus any increase from step 3. You and
   the source each roll **Negotiation against the other's Intelligence**.
   The winner moves the price **5% per net success** in their favor.
   *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: Halfway through this period, face-to-face negotiations to determine the actual cost take place
pitting their Negotiations Skill Ratings against each other's Intelligence

code.snippet: return { time, halfway: time / 2, found: true };

entries.text:
5. **Pick up.** If you won't pay, the deal is off, and the GM may raise the
   Availability TN next time you use that contact. *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: gamemasters can adjust the Availability target number upward the next time the character searches for something through that contact

entries.note: The deal being off if you won't pay is a card nobody presses (nothing is charged until 💴). Raising the Availability TN for that contact next time is not tracked.

entries.text: ### The book's example  *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: She wants to buy it on the street. The whip has an Availability of 24/14 days, with a Street Index of 3

entries.text:
Cheshire wants a **monofilament whip**: Availability **24/14 days**,
Street Index **3**, Cost **3,000¥**. None of her contacts come close to TN

pdf.quote: That means she'll be waiting 24 extra days (2 x 12 = 24)
That makes the cost a whopping 12,600

entries.text:
24. She puts the word out, cutting the TN to **12**. That adds **24 days**
(2 × 12) and **+1.2** Street Index. She rolls 2 successes: (24 + 14) ÷ 2 =
**19 days**. The price is 3,000 × 4.2 = **12,600¥**. She wins the
negotiation by 4, which is 20% off, and pays **10,080¥**.

pdf.quote: That means she'll be waiting 24 extra days (2 x 12 = 24)
That makes the cost a whopping 12,600

entries.text: ### Example: an Ares Predator
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
- **Ares Predator**: 9M, SA, **Availability 3/24 hrs**, Cost **450¥**,
  Street Index **.5**, Legality **6P-E**. *(SR3 p.278)*
entries.reason: The Ares Predator's row in the Heavy Pistols table (9M, SA, 450¥, Availability 3/24 hrs, Street Index .5, Legality 6P-E) cannot be read row by row from the text layer — the table columns come out as separate lists. The shipped pack matches the guide (packs-src/sr3e-sr3-firearms/ares-predator: 9M, SA, 3/24hrs, 450, .5); the Legality Code is not stored on the item.

entries.text:
- An Etiquette Test against **TN 3** scores 2 successes, so the pistol turns
  up in **12 hours**.

pdf.quote: The base time divided by the number of successes provides the actual time it takes the source to locate the item

entries.text:
- The asking price is 450 × .5 = **225¥** before negotiation. Its Street
  Index is below 1, so heavy pistols are cheaper on the street than in a
  store.

pdf.quote: The asking street price for gear is equal to the Cost of the item multiplied by the Street Index

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Life with a SIN vs. Living SINless".
> - The **Fake SIN price table was invented**. In SR3 a fake ID is a forged
>   credstick, and its rating sets its price: **Rating × Rating × 1,000¥** at
>   ratings 1–4, rising steeply after that. The table is below.
> - A SIN is not a "12-digit alphanumeric code". The book says the number is
>   **generated from personal data**, and police can read your birth date,
>   state of origin and initials from it.
> - "30–40% of the population is SINless" appears in no SR3 book checked.
> - There's no "Lesser / Greater Magical Permit". In the UCAS and CAS, magic
>   of **Force 3 or more** is regulated and needs a permit. Unregistered
>   spells, spirits and foci fall under legality category **(T) Class E
>   Magic**.
> - Permits **require a valid SIN**, and a fake one must beat a Rating 6
>   verification system.

pdf.quote: Availability Rating/24 hours Rating/72 hours Rating/14 days Rating/30 days Street Index 1 1 1 1
The actual numbers that compose a SIN are generated by a complex formula from several pieces of personal data
If using a fake ID (see p. 239) to purchase a permit, the ID must beat a Rating 6 verification system in an Opposed Test

entries.note: Composite errata callout. Checked against the book: a forged credstick's price is Rating × Rating × 1,000¥ at ratings 1-4 (p.239) and rises after that; SIN numbers are generated from personal data (p.238); Force 3+ magic is regulated with permits (MitS p.11); Class E Magic covers unregistered spells, spirits and foci (p.274); permits need a valid SIN and a fake must beat a Rating 6 system (p.274). The '30-40% of the population is SINless' claim is an absence claim I did not search for. None of this is modelled in the system.

  register. People living in the UCAS without one are "probationary
  citizens": they can't vote and have few or no civil rights.

entries.text: ## Life with a SIN  *(SR3 p.238–239)*
entries.reason: Section heading citing SR3 pp.238-239, over background text about SINs and credsticks with no mechanical counterpart in the system.

entries.text:
You need a SIN to get a legal job, open a bank account, own property, go to
school, rent an apartment, set up utilities, and travel legally, which
includes **buying a bus ticket**. Your credstick carries your ID, licenses
and permits, and can hold your fingerprints, palmprints and retinal prints.

inventory, and possibly video footage, and stores that realize they sold to
shadowrunners will hand those records to the police. *(SR3 p.273)*

entries.text: ### Magic and the law
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
- In the UCAS and CAS, **any spell, spirit, focus or other magical effect of
  Force 3 or higher is legally regulated**, though permits can be had. A
  felony committed with magic always counts as **premeditated**. *(MitS p.11)*
entries.reason: Legal background with no code counterpart. Checked against MitS printed p.11: Force 3 or higher magic is regulated in the UCAS and CAS with permits available, and a felony committed with magic is always premeditated. The guide agrees.

entries.text:

  unregistered spells, spirits and foci. *(SR3 p.274)*

pdf.quote: Class E Magic refers to unregistered spells, spirits, and foci

entries.text:
- Reading astral signatures is accepted forensic evidence, like fingerprints
  or DNA. *(MitS p.11)*
entries.reason: Legal background with no code counterpart. Checked against MitS printed p.11: reading astral signatures has the same status as fingerprinting or DNA testing in forensic science. The guide agrees.

> so spreading the risk makes sense.
